projectOutComesReport:
The Student Research Workshop was held in conjunction with ACL 2020. The SRW gives student researchers in Computational Linguistics and Natural Language Processing the opportunity to present their work and receive constructive feedback and mentorship by experienced members in ACL community.

 Website

We created a website, the primary source of information about the SRW: https://sites.google.com/view/acl20studentresearchworkshop/.

Additionally, we managed a Twitter account for posting updates to social media: (@acl_srw).

The call for papers was publicized through the ACL mailing list as well as the ACL 2020 Twitter account (@acl_meeting).

Mentoring Programs

We offered two mentoring programs this year. Pre-submission mentoring was available to all authors who wanted feedback before submitting their papers to the SRW. Post-acceptance mentoring program was available to authors of accepted papers, to get feedback on their camera-ready drafts and their conference presentations.

Pre-submission mentoring

We followed last year’s SRW in offering an optional round of pre-submission mentoring. Authors who submitted their papers in time for the pre-submission deadline received feedback from their assigned mentors before the final submission deadline, giving them time to integrate the mentor’s feedback into their final submission. A total of 57 papers participated in the pre-submission mentoring program. We recruited 30 mentors, all of whom are well-experienced researchers in the field, for the pre-submission program.

Papers were matched to mentors based on research areas. The mentoring feedback was sent to authors anonymously through the SRW organizers. Additionally, the majority of mentors also offered to participate in follow-up discussions with the authors directly via email until the main submission deadline.

Post-acceptance mentoring

Each accepted paper was assigned a post-acceptance mentor, to provide feedback to the authors about their camera-ready drafts and conference presentations (which were pre-recorded this year). 49 mentors were recruited, i.e., one for each accepted paper.

Grammarly Premium

During both the pre-submission and post-acceptance mentoring programs, writing assistance in the form of vouchers for one month's free use of Grammarly Premium was sent to all participating authors. These were provided by the ACL 2020 Diversity and Inclusion Committee.

Submission and Reviewing

Submission procedure

The SRW consisted of two submission tracks: research papers and thesis proposals. Research papers were intended to encompass completed work, as well as works-in-progress from graduate students, masters students, and advanced undergraduates. Thesis proposals were intended to be a venue for senior graduate students to get feedback on their thesis proposal and the broader ideas surrounding the appropriateness and impact of their chosen topic. 

Submissions were managed through the START conference system.

Number of submissions

We received 137 submissions in total: 10 thesis proposals and 127 research papers. Among these, 12 research papers were non-archival.

The SRW received submissions from students in 28 countries, with the majority of submissions coming from the United States, China, India, and Japan.

We accepted 49 papers, with an acceptance rate of 36%. After withdrawals and excluding non-archival papers, 42 papers appear in the SRW proceedings, including 6 thesis proposals and 36 research papers.

Because of changes in conference deadlines resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic, several authors requested a change from the non-archival to archival track. 

All accepted papers (archival and non-archival) were presented at the conference.

Program committee

We were fortunate to recruit 262 members for the SRW Program Committee. Each paper was assigned 3 reviewers. No reviewer was assigned more than 2 papers.

Reviewing

We based the review form on the ACL 2020 format, removing the questions about presentation type and best paper award: https://acl2020.org/_pages/docs/ACL_2020_Submission_Form.pdf

Virtual Conference

The SRW papers are presented in conjunction with other ACL main conference papers from July 6 to July 8. All the papers accepted to the SRW i.e., research papers and thesis proposals in both the archival and non-archival tracks, were presented at the conference.

For the virtual presentations, we adopted the same format as the main conference, which featured pre-recorded talks, live Q&A sessions, and online messaging channels.

The SRW is traditionally held as a poster session at the same time and venue as that of the main conference. In coordination with the ACL Program Chairs, the Virtual Infrastructure Chairs, and the Publication Chairs, the SRW was conducted as a track within the main virtual conference:

  • The virtual ACL website had the SRW papers in a separate track, listed alongside those of the main conference and system demonstrations.
  • The live Q&A sessions for SRW papers were in the same time slots as the papers of the main conference.
  • The schedule for the main conference included SRW papers.

SlidesLive was used to host the pre-recorded presentations. Authors were required to record a 12 minute video for each paper.

Each paper was assigned two one-hour live Q&A sessions. Since the authors are located in different time zones, we conducted a survey about their available time slots, and tried to schedule the Q&A sessions according to their preferences.

abstractText:
Massive high-dimensional data are ubiquitous in many scientific and engineering disciplines, such as bioinformatics, computer vision, neuroimaging, and signal processing. This proposal is motivated by emerging tools for analyzing data from these disciplines, such as nonsmooth, manifold-based learning with high-dimensional and multidimensional data. Building on the synergy among statistics, machine learning, and optimization, this research will focus on the development of new optimization algorithms and theory for nonsmooth manifold optimization. The project will also build on existing optimization strengths to develop new methods and theory in statistics and machine learning. Software packages will be developed to make the research outcomes readily available to other researchers and practitioners. In addition, the project will enhance the future technical workforce through the training of graduate students. 

It is known that statistical modeling of high-dimensional data may include the non-smooth regularization in the objective function, and some may even involve non-convex manifold constraints such as orthogonality constraints. The manifold-based learning offers a powerful framework for dimension reduction and signal processing. The combination of non-smooth regularization and non-convex manifold constraints brings new opportunities and challenges for designing optimization algorithms with convergence guarantees and also for developing new statistical methods and theory. The research outcomes of this project will provide new powerful analytic tools in nonsmooth manifold-based learning with theoretical guarantees. Software packages will be developed to make the research outcomes readily available to other researchers and practitioners.

abstractText:
The current pandemic has stimulated a strong response on the part of local, state, and federal government, with containment largely achieved through stringent lockdowns, effectively quarantining nearly every household in the country.  Given the enormous socio-economic impacts of this approach, it is imperative to understand how to minimize the spread of the epidemic while also minimizing deleterious effects and maximizing the availability of critical health resources.  This project seeks to address this challenge by devising a better and scalable alternative to lockdown under suitable constraints.

This project focuses on developing models for the COVID-19 pandemic, in particular looking at neighboring community spread, mitigation measures, and optimal distribution of healthcare resources in that context.  This project aims to (i) devise a better and scalable alternative to full lockdown; (ii) devise a cognitive solution that can be applied to various demographics having heterogeneous connectivity and population distribution with minimal information regarding previous epidemic spread; and (iii) minimize the impact of epidemic model uncertainties on the confinement and medical resource allocation strategies. The PIs will employ a collection of novel mathematical techniques to the problem that can handle heterogeneity and are scalable. The interdisciplinary team includes Johns Hopkins University, which has been a major Center for the collection of COVID-19 data.

projectOutComesReport:
The emergence of deadly viruses like AIDS, measles, SARS, Ebola, H1N1 influenza, and Tuberculosis has transformed the human race in recent decades, causing millions of deaths and long-term health issues. The impact of pandemics in today's interconnected world is exceptionally high in terms of human lives and financial burden. The ongoing SARS-2 COVID-19 outbreak has been declared a pandemic by the World Health Organization (WHO).

To contain the COVID-19 pandemic, governments and public health organizations have implemented various measures such as mandatory mask usage, lockdowns, social distancing, restricted travel, and vaccine mandates. The enforcement and effectiveness of these measures depend on factors like demographics, population density, availability of personal protective equipment (PPE), regional variants of COVID-19, and people's compliance.

Addressing the variability of demographic factors requires tailored containment strategies, considering the impact of neighboring areas. Confining the pandemic while minimizing economic repercussions is a complex task. Existing studies lack effective ways to contain the spread using minimal resources.

To tackle this challenge, a game-theoretic optimization solution is proposed. Game theory provides a framework for understanding disease spread and control policies. It involves the defender (government) aiming to minimize losses caused by the attacker (COVID-19 virus). By modeling game theory, an optimal outcome for control strategies can be identified. A demography-aware confinement strategy is proposed, incorporating game theory, demographic information, population distribution, mobility, economic constraints, and public health requirements.

 Adaptability to new COVID-19 variants is crucial, and a confinement model is developed by considering dynamic infection rates and epidemic characteristics. The extended strategy incorporates external factors and extends the SEIRV/D model.

 Applying game theory on a large scale, such as considering each state in the US, presents challenges and time constraints. Graph learning is employed to create nodes representing each state and build a graph database, replicating real-world conditions. This approach allows identification of crucial connections and modifying them to restrict mobility between states, affecting the spread of COVID-19. The proposed demography- and mobility-aware confinement policy-making system can reduce the infection rate of each state by over 50%.

Analyzing US government policies is crucial to mitigate the spread. Economic and health indicators, containment strategies, and stringency measures are considered in evaluating the government's response to COVID-19. Accurate predictions and insights can help manage the ongoing pandemic effectively.

A website is developed to provide visualizations of COVID-19 data, offering an interactive platform to access key statistics and trends. The user-friendly interface aims to enhance public understanding and facilitate informed decision-making. The website provides up-to-date information on infection rates, hospitalizations, vaccination progress, and other relevant metrics.

In summary, efforts include proposing a demography- and mobility-aware confinement strategy using game theory, evaluating US government response, and developing a website for data visualization to empower individuals and communities in combating the spread of COVID-19.

abstractText:
During tissue culture, plant genomes undergo frequent unexpected changes resulting in plants with different characteristics, called somaclonal variants. At lower frequency, similar variants called sports arise during normal growth. These new variants can have great economic value, but relatively little is known of the causes, nature and evolutionary significance of these phenomena. This project will investigate these changes in potato. The methods suitable to analyze these genomic changes will be applicable to other crops, and will be made available to the scientific and plant breeding community.  Societal impact is expected along two lines. First, this project will address a largely ignored potential source of variation likely to affect leading economic species. Second, the project entails several outreach activities, with two objectives: 1) Familiarize young students in underrepresented communities with science studies and careers and 2) Train advanced students and professionals in genomic approaches applicable to plant breeding. These objectives will be achieved through a combination of publishing in outreach journals, provision of international workshops, and production of learning videos.

The long term goal of this project is to understand the mechanisms and outcomes of genome instability and restructuring. The central hypothesis is that instability, while often deleterious, can also reshape the genome in ways that are less disruptive and potentially adaptive, such as by causing change or loss of heterozygosity, and dosage variation. Elucidating the causes, mechanisms, and consequences of these changes will help clarify their role in natural and artificial selection, and inform prediction, identification and, if appropriate, exploitation of these changes. The work will focus on the autotetraploid potato genome, in which we have documented extensive genomic changes in tissue culture regenerated potatoes, ranging from aneuploidy to indels, extreme rearrangements, but also more subtle changes in heterozygosity consistent with homologous DNA repair. Analysis of variation in potato suggests that genome instability varies according to environment and that it can occur during normal growth. The specific aims are to: i) Characterize the molecular patterns associated with somaclonal variation in potato. By examining resulting rearrangements, hypotheses on potential mechanisms, such as homologous vs. nonhomologous repair of dsDNA breaks, will be tested, ii) Study molecular patterns associated with differentiation of potato clones. Genomic analysis of clonally propagated potato will test the hypothesis that somatic homologous recombination results in variation and, iii) Investigate relation of dsDNA breaks to loss of heterozygosity. This objective will leverage induced and spontaneous loss of heterozygosity models to test possible mechanisms of dsDNA break repair, such as mitotic crossover and break-induced recombination.

projectOutComesReport:
Many cultivated plants are propagated vegetatively. For example, grapevine by cuttings and potato by tubers. During propagation, novel and valuable variants called sports can emerge. This project, funded by NSF award 1956429, aimed at characterizing the molecular mechanisms that underlie clonal variation. Our work has resulted in several key outcomes:


Understanding of how mutation rates vary in the plant growth apex:
The plant body develops from the Shoot Apical Meristem (SAM), which comprises three distinct morphogenetic layers: L1, L2, and L3. The L1 forms the epidermis, the L2 the photosynthetic tissue and gametes, and the L3 the adventitious roots and vascular system. We found that mutations accumulated differentially in the L1 versus the L2+L3, which appear homogeneous. Remarkably, the L1 accumulates more mutations than the L2+L3. As a result, the epidermis is genetically more unstable while the gametes are more stable. The differential accumulation of mutations among the layers helps explain the formation of layer chimeras, some of which have important implications for clonal breeding. Another finding was that mutations accumulated during protoplast regeneration (a possible step in plant manipulation) are often caused by reactive oxygen species, suggesting that cells in the SAM are protected from DNA damage caused by reactive oxygen species.. 

Characterizing the molecular basis of clonal variation: 
We focused on Russet Norkotah (RN), the most important US fresh market potato variety. Several RN clonal variants are widely grown due to their increased vigor and yield.. We sequenced the genome of four popular variants and found that all four displayed a novel allele of a gene called CYCLING DOF FACTOR 1 (CDF1 ). > The new alleles, formed through the excision of a transposable element, resulted in increased expression of CDF1 and delayed tuber maturity, explaining the improved performance of these clonal variants. By providing the likely molecular basis of RN clonal performance, this discovery could contribute to the breeding of new potato varieties.  

Characterizing the molecular basis of twin spot formation:
Homologous recombination during plant growth is important for both basic research and practical applications like gene replacement. However, its frequency and the molecular conditions that promote it remain poorly characterized. Certain plant heterozygotes for a leaf color gene form green-white twin spots on yellow-green leaves. Because each spot displays a homozygous phenotype, these occurrences have often been attributed to homologous recombination between chromosome pairs, resulting in somatic crossovers. Our genomic analyses determined that the twin spots formed by tobacco heterozygous for the sulfur mutation (Su/su), resulted not from homologous recombination but rather from chromosomal breakage, nonhomologous translocation, and aneuploidy. The ratio of the Su - su alleles determined color. This discovery extends our understanding of the mechanisms that alter the genome during plant growth and indicates that somatic recombination between the two chromosomes of a pair is rare. 

Broader Impacts:
The project produced educational videos and articles on general and plant genetics, as well as plant breeding, targeted at students ranging from junior high to college level. 

Products and Dissemination:
We have published several articles in refereed journals both describing the primary research and reviewing the significance of the research. We identified and resolved a material mix-up within the USDA potato collection. Team members have presented results in multiple conferences and seminars.  

Future Directions:
We plan to continue studying the effect of SAM layer organization on other important properties of the genome such DNA methylation and transposon regulation. In addition, we plan to elucidate the practical implications of SAM layer organization for the genetic modification of crops.

abstractText:
Information technology advances quickly and the computer science knowledge base expands dramatically along with it. These bring about new interconnections, challenges and opportunities in cybersecurity education. Two main educational themes resulting from these changes are interactive learning and dynamic/adaptive computer science course curricula. E-voting is a unique technology with rich (even conflicting) features that play roles in education related to these educational themes. Recent studies show that lessons based on E-voting technology enhance student learning outcomes when used in the classroom. This project aims to build an Electronic Voting Technology Inspired Interactive Teaching and Learning Framework for Cybersecurity Education that will effectively improve student learning outcomes and meet the needs of dynamic/adaptive computer science course curricula. 

This project addresses cybersecurity education by using e-voting as a basis. It emphasizes student-centered interactive learning by developing and using composable and interactive modules. The composable security topic modules allow an instructor to form a comprehensive or light-weighted information security curriculum or to integrate security topics into other courses. It can support dynamic/adaptive computer science course curricula. The interactive teaching and learning modules enable student-centered extensive and deep interactive learning, e.g., student-centered interactions and full engagement in the entire learning process and systematic inter-connection/transition among different teaching and learning activities and between topics. It supports broader teaching and learning activities not only within the classroom but also outside the classroom, not only involving class lecturing, but also involving class projects. It supports six student-centered interactions between the instructor and students, between students and students, and between students and the E-voting system. As a result, the project significantly enhances student learning outcomes in cybersecurity. It will attract more students, even undergraduates, underrepresented student groups and/or high school students, to the cybersecurity field and lead more undergraduate/minority/high school students to security research.

projectOutComesReport:
This project developed an Electronic Voting Technology-Inspired Interactive Teaching and Learning Framework for Cybersecurity Education. Drawing upon globally practiced and widely recognized voting and election systems—as well as the underlying e-voting technologies—this framework uses these real-world systems as both an entry point and an integrative element across teaching and learning activities. It aims to spark students’ interest in cybersecurity and foster meaningful engagement throughout their learning process.

The project designed an adaptive, composable, and modularizable cybersecurity curriculum that addresses the needs of dynamic and evolving computer science education. Its modular design allows instructors to create either a comprehensive or lightweight information security curriculum, or to seamlessly integrate security topics into other courses. This flexibility supports rapidly changing educational requirements in computer science and cybersecurity. Notably, the curriculum has been successfully aligned with two widely accepted frameworks: ACM/IEEE CSEC2017 and DHS/NSA Cybersecurity Knowledge Units.

To complement the curriculum, the project implemented an adaptive plug-and-play interactive teaching and learning platform. This platform enables students to build and test various components—both large and small—of a distributed system involving multiple voter clients and tallying servers. The system includes default components that facilitate integration and experimentation. It promotes extensive, deep, and student-centered interactive learning through full engagement in the entire educational process, including transitions between activities and topics. The platform supports a wide range of educational settings—both inside and outside the classroom—and includes class lectures, hands-on projects, and collaborative work. It enables six forms of student-centered interaction: between instructor and students, among students, and between students and the e-voting system.

The developed framework and implemented platform are closely integrated and mutually reinforcing, forming a cohesive ecosystem for cybersecurity education.

The project has generated significant and well-recognized outcomes, with results widely accepted by the cybersecurity education community. These have been published in prominent venues such as the ACM SIGCSE Technical Symposium (including the Best Paper Award at SIGCSE 2023) and the IFIP WISE conferences.

The framework has been successfully used in several cybersecurity courses at Indiana University Indianapolis (formerly Indiana University Purdue University Indianapolis) and at University of California, Davis, each taught by one of the two project PIs. Additionally, the lead PI has been invited to present the framework to faculty at multiple institutions, including the University of Alabama, University of Texas at Arlington, and Purdue University. The system has also been demonstrated to diverse audiences from academia, industry, and government.

The project has also resulted in one U.S. patent (US 2025/0104500 A1, pending).

In summary, the project has produced a practical and impactful cybersecurity curriculum and interactive plug-and-play learning platform, both of which significantly enhance student learning outcomes in cybersecurity education.

abstractText:
COVID-19, the disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus, is at the center of one of the most dangerous pandemics the world has ever known. As it spreads through the human population the virus mutates producing proteins that can lead to higher infection rates (infectivity), and an increased ability to cause severe disease (virulence). This project will predict the most likely mutations of the virus by combining methods from machine learning, mathematics and biophysics.   Specifically, the proteins resulting from viral mutations will be experimentally synthesized, and their infectivity and virulence will be tested by the project team through a collaboration with researchers in industry. This project benefits from unprecedented access to genomic data compiled on SARS-CoV-2, combined with a rich set of novel tools developed through interdisciplinary advances in data science, mathematics, and biophysics. The results of this project will build a pipeline capable of assisting the development of vaccines and drugs against COVID-19 while simultaneously advancing the fields of machine learning and mathematical virology. The project team is led by mathematicians, molecular biologists and biotechnology experts working in an interdisciplinary and collaborative setting. Students and postdoctoral researchers will be trained and will participate in publicly disseminating the findings and results of the project.

 
The SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus is believed to have originated as a bat virus and to have evolved through a combination of sequence mutations, recombination, and natural selection to be infectious in human hosts. Some of the most relevant sequence variations occurred in the S gene encoding the Spike (S) protein. As SARS-CoV-2 spreads through the human population, mutations of the S gene can potentially increase viral infectivity and virulence. Within the framework of an evolutionary algorithm, the PIs will combine graph theory, topological data analysis, and computational biophysics to characterize the most likely mutations of the S protein. This powerful interdisciplinary approach will draw upon existing experimental data from SARS-CoV-2. The PIs will collaborate with an industrial partner to experimentally design the peptides corresponding to those predicted sequences, and  use binding affinity assays and cryo-electron microscopy to test binding of the peptides to the human receptor (ACE2). The resulting pipeline will help us better understand the evolutionary landscape of viral proteins and will assist researchers in the development of anti-viral drugs and vaccines. Future extensions of this work will increase our understanding of how viruses are transmitted across species and propagate in humans. The project will provide multi-disciplinary student and postdoctoral training. The PIs will broadly disseminate their results, as well as the data they collect and software they design.

With this award, the Mathematical Biology Program in the Division of Mathematical Sciences and the Chemistry of Life Processes Program in the Division of Chemistry are supporting Drs. Arsuaga, Rodriguez, and Vazquez from University of California-Davis to study genomic variations of the SARS-CoV-2 viral spike (S) protein and predict the expansion range of transmission in human populations.

This grant is being awarded using funds made available by the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act supplemental funds allocated to MPS.

orgLongName: Directorate for Mathematical and Physical Sciences
program: RAPID, COVID-19 Research
projectOutComesReport:
The COVID-19 pandemic, a public health crisis that spanned several years and touched on every aspect of our society, was caused by the coronavirus SARS-CoV2. Infection by this virus starts when its spike (S) protein binds to a host cell. Mutations in the S protein appeared as the virus spread through the human population, sometimes leading to higher infection rates and an increased ability to cause severe disease. This RAPID award supported the development of methods to predict the most likely mutations of SARS-CoV2. Specifically, we combined methods from mathematics, machine learning and biophysics to predict mutations in the S protein that would be more likely to increase infectivity of a human host.  We started collaborations with other scientists to experimentally synthesize viral proteins of interest and test their binding affinity to human receptors. As a result of this project we built an interdisciplinary pipeline to predict mutations in coronaviruses that can cause higher infectivity. 

An important challenge in vital evolution is to identify non-human animal coronaviruses that may infect humans. To tackle this problem we created an artificial neural network model that learns from the binding of the S protein of alpha and beta coronaviruses to their host receptor. This model produces a human-Binding Potential (h-BiP) score that can distinguish the binding potential among human coronaviruses with high accuracy. We used this model to identify two previously unknown viruses, Bat coronavirus BtCoV/133/2005 and Rhinolophus affinis coronavirus isolate LYRa3, which have the potential to bind human receptors. Importantly the model predicted that the S protein of SARS-CoV2 woudl bind a human receptor. This approach shows that machine learning methods can be used to predict host expansion events and can be used for surveillance of novel coronaviruses. [https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.12.11.520008v1.abstract]

In a separate subproject and in collaboration with a group of biophysicists at UC Davis, we used AlphaFold to predict the structures of the furin enzyme with known six residue inhibitory peptides. This approach was used to study the wild type furin cleavage domain for the virus and several mutants. We found that the delta variant has a high binding strength with the furin enzyme. This information can be used to inform the development of drugs that target the furin enzyme and prevent the spread of the virus. [https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.01.04.475011v1.abstract]

Our work has significant implications for advancing our understanding of the evolutionary landscape of viral proteins, viral transmission, and propagation in humans. Our interdisciplinary approach, combining data science, mathematics, and biophysics, has the potential to aid in drug development.

Throughout the project, we have been committed to training students researchers in interdisciplinary research and disseminating their findings to the public. We contributed to the education of young researchers by training 15 undergraduates, two graduate students, and three high school students, providing them with hands-on research experience. We helped organize an NSF-sponsored undergraduate research conference on the mathematical modeling of COVID-19. This conference provided a platform for young researchers to present their work and exchange ideas with experts in the field. Members of our team presented their research to a variety of audiences and in various formats, including conferences, webinars, and seminars. Results of the research are reported in two research papers (submitted for publication), one undergraduate thesis and one PhD thesis.

abstractText:
The Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU) program "Pure and Applied Mathematics at UC Davis" hosted by the Department of Mathematics at UC Davis will provide early training in mathematics research for leaders in the mathematical sciences. The program will broadly cover the research areas of the mathematics department, including both pure and applied mathematics. Recruitment of women, underrepresented minorities, and students with disadvantaged backgrounds will be emphasized. The program will accept 12 students each year, who will work under the supervision of UC Davis mathematics faculty, and in collaboration with postdoctoral fellows and graduate students. The research training will include a lecture on ethics in the mathematical sciences, and field trips to sites in the Bay Area. Students will be encouraged present their results at mathematics conferences and local venues after the summer program. 
 
On a multi-year basis, the UC Davis Math REU will cover most of the research areas of the mathematics department.  These areas include mathematical biology, probability, geometry/topology, algebra, combinatorics, partial differential equations, applied mathematics, and quantum mathematics. Four to six projects will be offered every year with at least two students recruited to each project, for a total of 12 students per year.  The program will be evaluated with formative and summative assessments, and program organizers will stay in contact with students after each summer ends.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
The REU Site: Pure and Applied Mathematics at UC Davis was designed to train undergraduate students in mathematical research across a broad range of areas, including algebra, topology, mathematical biology, fluid dynamics, and quantum information. The overarching goal of the program was to inspire and prepare undergraduate students to pursue careers in the mathematical sciences by combining rigorous research experiences with professional development, mentorship, and community building.

The project began during the COVID-19 pandemic, which required postponing the first cohort. During this initial period, the investigators focused on developing the intellectual and organizational infrastructure of the program. Faculty mentors were recruited, and the first set of research projects was selected, spanning both pure and applied mathematics. A dedicated REU website and application system were created, and extensive national outreach efforts were conducted. Although no students were hosted during this first year, these efforts enabled the successful launch and long-term stability of the program.

In subsequent years, the REU program developed into a highly competitive and impactful training environment. The first cohort hosted 13 students selected from a national pool of 155 applicants, and in later years the number of applicants increased significantly to over 300, reflecting growing visibility and demand for the program. Students participated in faculty-led research projects covering a wide range of topics in modern mathematics, and each participant completed a written research report and delivered an oral presentation at the end of the program.

A defining feature of the program was its integrated structure combining research, mentoring, and professional development. Students lived in shared housing arrangements that fostered collaboration and peer learning, and they engaged in regular interactions with faculty, graduate students, and postdoctoral researchers. Weekly activities included research discussions, informal mentoring sessions, and community-building events. The program also provided exposure to ethical issues in science, interdisciplinary research, and career pathways through invited talks, workshops, and interactions with researchers from academia and industry. Technical training sessions in programming and mathematical writing were part of the program.

The REU produced significant outcomes in terms of student research and dissemination. All participants completed original research projects, many of which were presented at national conferences and undergraduate research symposia. Several students continued to present their work after the program, including at the Joint Mathematics Meetings and other professional venues. These dissemination activities demonstrate the program’s effectiveness in preparing students to communicate mathematical research to broader audiences.

One of the most significant impacts of the program was its contribution to the pipeline of students entering graduate programs in the mathematical sciences. A substantial number of participants went on to pursue graduate study at leading institutions, including UC San Diego, University of Chicago, Stanford University, UCLA, and others. Several students received prestigious awards and fellowships, including NSF Graduate Research Fellowships and international scholarships. Other participants continued into careers in industry, education, and interdisciplinary scientific fields, demonstrating the broad applicability of the skills developed through the program.

The program also made important contributions to broadening participation in mathematics. Recruitment efforts targeted a wide range of institutions, including liberal arts colleges, the cohorts included students from diverse academic and demographic backgrounds. The program emphasized inclusive mentoring practices and created a collaborative environment.

Overall, the UC Davis Mathematics REU successfully established a robust model for undergraduate research training. Despite initial disruptions due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the program trained dozens of students, produced meaningful research outcomes, and contributed significantly to the development of the next generation of mathematical scientists. The integration of research, mentorship, and community-building proved particularly effective in supporting student success and fostering long-term engagement with the mathematical sciences.

abstractText:
Stripe rust is a devastating fungal disease that threatens global wheat production, with estimated global losses of around 1 billion dollars per year. Recently, the WTK1 gene was identified from a wild wheat relative that provides broad-spectrum resistance against the fungal pathogen causing stripe rust. Despite the importance of this disease, how WTK1 confers disease resistance remains unknown. This project will focus on identifying how WTK1 perceives the fungal pathogen causing stripe rust and signals inside wheat cells to confer disease resistance using cutting-edge protein-protein and genome editing technologies. A greater understanding of WTK1-mediated disease resistance will provide important mechanistic insight into signaling networks in plant disease resistance. A key goal of this project is to integrate research with the teaching and training of a diverse student body. As an NSF-BSF collaboration between Gitta Coaker and Tzion Fahima, funding will facilitate international US-Israel collaborations and opportunities for scientific training in both the US and Israel. The PI will also collaborate with a local middle school to develop hands-on plant laboratory modules that will utilize wheat genetics to illustrate the connection between genotype and phenotype. These laboratory modules will be implemented in the 7th grade science curriculum, will be inexpensive, sustainable, and reach >1,000 students during the course of the project. 

Stripe rust, caused by Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici (Pst), is a devastating fungal disease threatening global wheat production. The WTK1 resistance gene derived from wild emmer wheat provides broad-spectrum disease resistance against Pst. WTK1 encodes a protein with tandem kinase-pseudokinase domain architecture, which represents a novel protein family widespread across the plant kingdom. Experiments will investigate the importance of WTK1 domain architecture for conferring disease resistance to Pst as well as the identity of WTK1 associated proteins.  RNAseq will be used to investigate wheat responses in resistant and susceptible wheat genotypes (+/- WTK1). Imporatant-WTK1 associated proteins and signaling nodes will be investigated using genome editing approaches for their importance in wheat disease resistance against Pst. Collectively, these studies will shed light into the function of a novel protein family and mechanisms controlling broad-spectrum disease resistance in monocots.

jrnl.auth: Reveguk, Tamara and Fatiukha, Andrii and Potapenko, Evgenii and Reveguk, Ivan and Sela, Hanan and Klymiuk, Valentyna and Li, Yinghui and Pozniak, Curtis and Wicker, Thomas and Coaker, Gitta and Fahima, Tzion

program: NSF and US-Israel Binational Science Fou
projectOutComesReport:
Plant diseases caused by fungal pathogens threaten global food production. A recently recognized protein family —tandem kinase proteins (TKPs)—features a unique structure with two or more fused kinases. Kinases are involved in cellular signaling and TKPs confer resistance to devastating fungal pathogens. This project advanced our understanding of TKPs by contributing to a global TKP Atlas, which cataloged over 2,600 TKPs across 104 plant species. The TKP Atlas suggested that these proteins might play a broader role in plant defense than previously recognized, with potential to trap pathogen effectors.

To explore TKP function, we studied RWT4, a wheat TKP that provides resistance to the wheat blast fungus (Magnaporthe oryzae). RWT4 directly binds to a fungal effector protein, AvrPWT4, leading to activation of immune responses. This interaction is highly specific: RWT4 recognizes only the avirulent form of the effector, and defense activation depends on its kinase function and a unique structural region known as a partial kinase duplication. These discoveries showed for the first time that a TKP can act as a pathogen sensor, directly perceiving a pathogen protein resulting in disease resistance.

In parallel, we examined another TKP, WTK1, by performing transcriptional profiling after fungal infection in wheat. This provided key insight into the downstream signaling events triggered by TKP activation, including the induction of defense genes and cell death responses associated with immune protection.

Beyond the core scientific discoveries, the project made meaningful broader impacts. We developed and implemented laboratory modules for middle school STEM education, introducing young students to plant immunity and biotechnology. Undergraduate researchers were integral to the project, gaining hands-on experience in molecular cloning, gene expression analysis, and protein biochemistry. Their training contributes to the next generation of scientists equipped to address agricultural and biological challenges. We strengthened international collaborations as this is a partnered grant with Israel.

By revealing how TKPs detect fungal pathogens and activate immunity, this research paves the way for developing and improving durable disease resistance in wheat and other crops. Understanding TKP structure and function opens new opportunities for sustainable agriculture at a time when plant diseases continue to threaten food security worldwide.

abstractText:
Rapid societal shifts associated with the COVID-19 pandemic have necessitated that education move online. Such shifts also increase students’ exposure to online discrimination, which can in turn negatively impact students’ academic performance and development. Prior research suggests that discrimination can push students away from pursuing STEM careers at a moment when a diverse, interdisciplinary STEM workforce is critical to confronting complex scientific challenges. In traditional in-person educational settings, positive interactions with diverse classmates and instructors can facilitate the maintenance of cognitive performance, educational attainment, and STEM participation despite negative experiences. Whether these positive interactions transfer to an online context, and whether they similarly buffer the effects of discrimination, is less understood. This study captures important daily variations in students’ well-being and academic outcomes that can inform future university practices regarding education and student wellness during crises. The findings may be of particular interest to educational institutions that have been forced to quickly shift to online instruction. As the COVID-19 pandemic demonstrates, there is a need for novel ideas and excellent leadership in STEM fields. This study will identify factors that may protect and promote STEM career outcomes.

This project capitalizes on an existing ethnically diverse sample of college STEM majors who previously (pre-pandemic) reported on their daily in-class experiences, well-being, and academic outcomes. The present study collects additional data, using nearly identical methods, across two 7-day cycles. The project aims to: (1) Describe the frequency of daily discrimination experienced by college-aged ethnically diverse STEM majors; (2) Assess the extent to which rates of discrimination differ from their pre-pandemic levels; (3) Examine whether daily discrimination is correlated with STEM students’ day-to-day well-being, academic efficacy, and outcome expectations for their future STEM careers; and (4) Explore digital peer and university social supports as moderators of associations between daily discrimination and outcomes in a context of limited in-person interaction. Exploratory open-ended questions will identify participants’ educational experiences related to COVID-19.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

program: COVID-19 Research, DS-Developmental Sciences, RAPID
projectOutComesReport:
With the country still reeling from of the devastating COVID-19 pandemic, including its long-term impact on national education and healthcare, young people need ample academic and socioemotional support. However, there is growing evidence that ethnic-racial minority youth and adults alike are instead being subjected to discrimination and unequal treatment, both interpersonally and via media. In this study, a diverse college-aged sample of STEM majors relayed their academic and personal experiences during this crisis. Furthermore, the longitudinal nature of our data allowed us to cross-reference these findings with students’ past reports of these factors prior to the COVID-19 pandemic. This work also uniquely provided the ability to study day-to-day stability and change in young people’s experiences across the pandemic and contexts.

To address this topic, we sought to examine a series of pointed and timely questions. First, what is the frequency of daily environmental and proximal microaggressions experienced by college-aged STEM students, including Asian American students and students who may have been vicariously or directly impacted by discrimination experiences during the pandemic? Second, how might these experiences impact minority youth’s stress day-to-day during and after student learning was shifted exclusively online. Third, what might be the mental and physical health impacts of environmental microaggressions among these students as compared to data collected from the same participants prior to the COVID-19 pandemic?

We assessed these questions through a variety of methods. We gathered an ethnically diverse sample of college students and administered to them daily electronic surveys. These surveys, containing quantitative and qualitative measures, inquired about students’ daily personal and academic experiences, and specifically how they might have changed since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic. Student surveys also included measures assessing their daily experiences during the pandemic of microaggressions, ethnic identity beliefs, diversity exposure, and other race- and discrimination-related perceptions and experiences.

Our initial findings indicate that most of the young people in our study reported experiencing some form of vicarious ethnic-racial discrimination at some point across the data collection waves. In addition, some study participants reported experiencing some form of direct ethnic-racial discrimination. However, in general these experiences were fairly low infrequency. Furthermore, we have begun to examine the qualitative data related to students online learning experiences during the pandemic. Both stressors and factors that were helpful in the learning process largely centered around social relationships with instructors and with peers. For example, eliciting social support from others and experiencing empathy and concern from instructors were particularly helpful to students.

These and a number of additional threads of research have been, and will continue to be, disseminated through presentations, writings, and our newly informed work with schools and student-supporting communities. Specifically, our planned and future manuscripts will be useful in fields such as education (e.g., STEM; higher ed), psychology, human development, and sociology. In addition, findings from our sample of college-aged STEM majors could directly relate to how institutions of higher education conduct their human resources practices in relation to student success and well-being. Moreover, the context of online education during the pandemic can provide additional insight as to how to best support ethnically/racially diverse STEM students who may engage in online learning. This project’s provided insights into students’ life experiences in relation to social ethnic-racial biases, and the outcomes thereof, will speak to each of these and other domains.

abstractText:
Many proteins function by relaying information of chemical activity at one site to a distant site on the same molecule. This simple concept of long-distance communication – collectively referred to as allostery – reverberates across much of biology by providing the most rapid, direct, and efficient means to switch proteins between functional and non-functional forms. But can such action-at-distance also arise when the two sites reside on different, but closely interacting, biological assemblies? This project seeks to address this question by experimentally investigating long-distance communication between cellular membranes and a ubiquitous protein called E-cadherin, which is embedded within these membranes. This project uses single-molecule measurements with model membranes and living cells to tease-out relations between the mechanical properties of the membrane and the molecular-level organization and function of E-cadherin. These studies will address how cell membranes control the reorganization of E-cadherins on the cell surface and consequently regulate cell interactions and cell migration during tissue formation and wound healing. The effort also provides benefit to the broader scientific community by establishing a new paradigm that links the global material properties of cellular membranes with biochemical behaviors of individual proteins. The work will (1) train graduate and undergraduate students in interdisciplinary collaborative research combining tools, techniques, and perspectives from membrane biophysics, single molecule science, soft matter, mechanobiology, and biochemistry and (2) implement proactive mechanisms to engage underrepresented minorities and contribute directly to enhancing diversity, inclusion, and equity with the STEM fields.  It thus integrates outreach, education, and research in basic interdisciplinary research at the interface between the physical and biological sciences.  

The researchers will address a central hypothesis that changes in membrane mechanical properties – such as those elicited by an upstream mechanical stimuli – can induce allosteric activation of embedded membrane proteins.  They will combine approaches, methodologies, and tools developed in single-molecule biophysics, functional protein dynamics, and membrane mechanics. Specifically, they will use (1) quantitative characterization methods including single molecule force - fluorescence microscopy, wide-field and high-content spinning disk confocal fluorescence microscopy, and phase contrast optical microscopy; (2) molecularly-tailored and mechanically activated membrane models (e.g., giant lipid vesicles subjected to well-defined osmotic stresses); and (3) living cells expressing fluorescently tagged, embedded membrane proteins. As a test-bed, the proposal investigates the force-induced clustering of  E-cadherin, a key cell-surface adhesion receptor,  which is essential in orchestrating complex movement of cells during tissue formation and in maintaining tissue integrity. The PI and co-PI will focus their efforts to  resolve key determinants of the force-induced protein clustering in a minimal model and establish biophysical determinants for allosteric protein clustering on live cell surfaces. Successful completion of this EAGER application will establish the experimental rules underlying membrane allostery, in the specific context of cell-cell adhesion.  These principals would be broadly applicable to membrane allostery across multiple aspects of cellular organization, dynamics, and function including signaling, homeostasis and adaptation, and mechanobiology. Even more generally, the insights obtained from this research should provide experimental data for determining whether global mechanical properties can influence properties of single molecules.

This award is supported by the Molecular Biophysics and Cellular Dynamics and Function clusters of Molecular and Cellular Biosciences.

jrnl.artTitl: Light Activated BioID (LAB): an optically activated proximity labeling system to study protein-protein interactions
jrnl.auth: Shafraz, Omer and Davis, Carolyn Marie Orduno and Sivasankar, Sanjeevi

orgLongName: Directorate for Biological Sciences
orgLongName2: Division of Molecular and Cellular Biosciences
program: EAGER, NANOSCALE BIO CORE
projectOutComesReport:
Molecular allostery represents a mode of molecular communication in biology where a perturbation or binding at a site on the molecule induces a conformational or functional change at another  topographically and stereo-specifically distinct site on the molecule.  This project sought to extend this concept beyond molecule to cellular membranes where a global mechanical perturbation alters local conformations or spatial distributions of cellular receptors (and thus functions). It also sought to use the project as a means to achieve broader impacts of graduate and post-doctoral training, involvement of undergraduate and under-represented minority researchers, and the development of teaching modules. 

Both intellectual merit and broader impacts were met. 

For the intellectual merit, the project resulted in two major outcomes. First, a new spatially and temporally targeted, high precision molecular technology, to discover novel membrane protein interactions in cells. We developed genetically encodable, light activated proximity labeling enzyme that can be switched ‘on’ or ‘off’ at predetermined cellular locations and time points using low intensity blue light (Shafraz, O., Davis, C.M.O., Sivasankar, S., (2023) Light Activated BioID (LAB): an optically activated proximity labeling system to study protein-protein interactions, J Cell Sci (2023) 136 (19): jcs261430.). The system enables quantitative mapping of interactions between membrane proteins in presence of external mechanical stimuli, such as needed to validate the notion of membrane allostery – the central goal of this EAGER project.  Second, we discovered how osmotically induced global mechanical deformations can spatially and temporally redistribute specific membrane molecules in localized niches and elicit new functionalities (Pallavi Sambre, Chris Carnahan, Atul N. Parikh, in preparation, 2024).   These findings are important in combining membrane mechanical deformations with protein interaction patterns needed to characterize membrane allostery.

For the broader impacts, the findings of the project suggest a new framework for understanding how global mechanical stimuli at the membrane level can translate into localized functional activation at the molecular level and offer a new proximity-based high precision molecular technology.  The project also contributed to the doctoral dissertation of Pallavi Sambre, a Materials Science graduate student, and provided post-doctoral training for Dr. Omer Shafraz.  The concept of allostery yielded a module for a graduate-level course on physical biology.

abstractText:
The exponential industrialization of space, in the form of tens of thousands of rather large Low Earth Orbit (LEO) communications satellites (LEOsats), has a timescale short compared with normal scientific research projects.  As they are presently configured, LEOsats will have a major deleterious impact on ground based optical astronomy.  This study will assess the science impact of LEOsats, and explore the effectiveness of different mitigation strategies.  There is an urgent need for informed studies that assess the impact realistically, as well as exploratory investigations to choose one, or a few, of the best of various proposed different mitigation strategies.  Since the Vera C. Rubin Observatory (VRO) is most impacted, with a domino effect on all other astronomy which would use VRO data, this project will focus on assessment, laboratory measurements, simulation, and mitigation, specific to the VRO and its initial mission, the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST).  The natural night sky is the universal heritage of everyone, not just professional astronomers, and it is threatened by tens of thousands of bright moving LEOsats.  Finding ways to reduce their impact affects the quality of life of pretty well all of modern society.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
PROJECT SUMMARY

Humanity is experiencing an exponential industrialization of space, in the form of tens of thousands of large Low Earth Orbit (LEO) communications satellites. This is happening on a timescale short compared with normal scientific research projects. Without mitigation, in the next several years this will transform ground based optical astronomy. We find that there is no combination of mitigations which can alleviate the negative impacts on astronomy science.

Intellectual Merit:

Given that several companies are going ahead with their satellite constellations, our options are limited to assessing the science impact, and exploration of the effectiveness of several mitigation strategies.   The Vera C. Rubin Observatory "Legacy Survey of Space and Time" (LSST) is most impacted, because of its wide and rapid survey of the night sky.  Negative impacts on LSST science will have a domino effect on all other astronomy which would use Rubin Observatory data, including space telescopes.

When satellites cross the wide field of view, they leave a trail on the image. These trails can cause so-called "systematic errors" in the science. This is true even if the trails are "masked" in sofware processing. We explored combinations of several mitigation options. During the two years of this grant, this exploration covered: LSST science impact assessment, lab measurements of the effects of satellite trails on the LSST Camera, forward simulation of Rubin Observatory sky survey imaging including synthetic satellite trails, and a number of mitigation options.  As an example, we worked with SpaceX on methods to make their satellites in orbit appear less bright.  Another example is advanced algorithms for LSST data analysis which may alleviate some of the damaging effects on LSST science due to satellite trails.

Broader Impacts:

We addressed the pressing need for more work on this new challenge to astronomy on several broad fronts on a short timescale. This is in addition to the work we continue to undertake supported by Vera Rubin Observatory Project personnel and some students in our group. Our work, reports, and workshops have had an impact on the satellite industry. There is a growing realization among satellite operators that they must pursue novel engineering solutions, and adopt best practices for making their satellites less visible. The postdoctoral scholar suppported by this grant is a hispanic minority.

This Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU) site award to the University of California-Davis, located in Davis, CA, supports the training of 28 total students for 10 weeks during the summers of 2020-2022. This program, supported by the Division of Chemistry in the Mathematical and Physical Sciences Directorate, engages students with research projects at the interface of energy, materials science and biotechnology. Participants also take part in interactive development workshops to improve scientific communication skills, provide career guidance, and bolster capacity to perform science in a professional setting. This site offers additional multi-level mentoring and resources to accommodate blind and vision-impaired students.

Students engage in unique research projects in energy-related, fundamental and applied chemistry with expert chemistry researchers. Examples of research projects include synthesis of molecular and heterogenous catalysts; fabrication of artificial photosynthesis devices from inexpensive nanomaterials; protein engineering and synthetic biology for biofuel production; and computational modeling and simulations for enzyme and catalyst design. Graduate school and professional development programs include seminars on the search for suitable graduate programs and identifying keys for success in graduate school and beyond. The site is committed to broadening participation in STEM by promoting participation of first-generation, underrepresented minority, blind and vision impaired, and female undergraduate students from local community colleges, primarily undergraduate institutions, and minority-serving institutions such as the University of Puerto Rico.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

In this project, funded by the REU Sites Program in the Chemistry Division of the National Science Foundation, Professors Jesus Velazquez and Annaliese Franz have developed the University of California, Davis ChemEnergy REU site. The program is designed to provide diverse undergraduate students with a unique ten-week research experience that emphasizes chemistry at the intersection of energy, materials chemistry, and biotechnology.

Our ChemEnergy REU site aims to create a collaborative cohort experience that bridges different chemistry disciplines, concentrating on the fundamentals and applications of energy, catalysis, and enzymes.The ChemEnergy REU program has the experience, resources, and multi-level mentoring necessary to support students who are blind or vision-impaired in their research endeavors. REU students in the program will gain 1) skills in critical thinking and science communication, 2) the ability to work effectively as part of a research team, and 3) an understanding of the broader implications of chemistry and its connections to real-world issues. Overall, the experience is designed to provide students with a solid foundation for future careers in chemistry and energy sciences.

Outcomes

The UC Davis ChemEnergy REU program (2020-2024), provided a diverse group of 30 undergraduate students—primarily from institutions that do not grant PhDs—with a research experience titled "Energy and Catalysis" in the Chemistry Department. This program facilitated cooperative learning among students and laboratories involved, fostered a cohort experience, and reinforced important academic and professional concepts aimed at creating a lasting impact on the students' education.

Each year, we recruited highly qualified students (average GPA = 3.7), with strong representation from underrepresented minorities (19/30, or 64%) and a gender balance (20 females, 10 males). We were able to offer an engaging program with robust components by collaborating with various opportunities provided for our NSF LSAMP, McNair, and UC-HBCU scholars at UC Davis. REU students participated in weekly seminars and workshops focused on professional development, presented by our faculty mentors. Students participated in an ice cream "happy hour" with the department, helping students feel integrated into our community. Workshop topics included "Getting into Graduate School," "Writing a Personal Statement," "Thriving and Surviving Graduate School," "Science Communication," and "How to Make a Poster." We organized a field trip to the Tahoe Environmental Research Center and held an REU Symposium featuring a poster session and a reception. Programming also included attending research group meetings and weekly one-on-one mentoring with graduate mentors and faculty.

More than half of the students presented their REU research at their home institutions upon returning. We provided funding to support their participation in regional and national ACS conferences. Several students presented at the ACS National Meetings, SACNAS, the Annual Biomedical Research Conference for Minority Students (ABRCMS), and the National Organization for the Professional Advancement of Black Chemists and Chemical Engineers (NOBBCChE). Some REU students received national awards, including NSF GRFP and ACS travel awards. Several publications now feature REU students as co-authors, listed above.

Throughout this program, we successfully supported students in developing their understanding of energy and catalysis, enhancing their professional development and communication skills, and fostering a sense of belonging within the chemistry community during these unprecedented times.

abstractText:
This Grant Opportunities for Academic Liaison with Industry (GOALI) project will support a research team to develop models for the loading placed on multiline ring anchors subjected to wind, waves and other forces. A Multiline Ring Anchor (MRA) is a ring-shaped anchor designed to be deeply embedded in offshore soils for the purposes of anchoring multiple floating platforms. The increase in offshore development in the wind energy, wave energy and aquaculture sectors requires multiple closely spaced nominally identical platforms that need this type of omni-directional anchor. This novel configuration differs substantially from the typical oil and gas installation and allows consideration of sharing anchors among multiple platforms, thereby driving down capital, material, fabrication and installation costs and duration significantly. Previous simulation-based research conducted by the research team has shown that this concept is feasible but that truly leveraging the advantages of multiline anchoring will require novel anchor designs that can be installed quickly and inexpensively and that also deliver omni-directional capacity and resistance to cyclic loading. To achieve this, the research team will develop models for the loading placed on the anchors from wind, waves and other forces; perform reduced-scale centrifuge tests to provide data on the behavior of MRA systems under these loads; and develop numerical models to assess the behavior of the anchors under multiple loading scenarios. This research project includes a collaboration with an industrial partner, Vryhof Anchors, to ensure that results are driven by the needs of industry and can move rapidly to further industry-driven technology development.

In order to demonstrate proof-of-concept for the MRA, a series of research tasks are planned that will quantify stochastic and time-varying loads placed on the anchor by wind, wave and aquaculture platforms. Additionally, the team will develop conceptual MRA designs based on finite element and plastic limit analysis and assess the suitability of the MRA for sand and clay conditions by a range of methods including centrifuge testing. These tasks will enable the development of fundamental understanding of the response of embedded anchors to cyclic and directionally varying loading. The team will deliver a system evaluation for realistic installations that will provide the impetus for further demonstration-scale research into the MRA. Fundamental advances in understanding the dynamics of interconnected offshore systems as well as the response of deeply embedded anchors in different types of soil to complex loading form the core of the intellectual merit.

projectOutComesReport:
The Multiline Ring Anchor (MRA) is a novel anchor designed to be deeply embedded in offshore soils for the purpose of anchoring multiple floating units suited to wind or wave energy extraction or aquaculture. This anchor is suitable for sand and clay seafloor conditions. The MRA combines features of existing anchor systems such as high geotechnical efficiency and capacity with ease of installation and delivers omni-directional capacity. It has the potential to dramatically increase the economy of offshore development for the provision of energy and food to the benefit of society. A key feature of the MRA is its potential for deployment in a shared-anchor system, which can further reduce capital costs for systems involving arrays of floating units. The goal of this project was to develop the MRA from a conceptual stage to a stage of full-scale prototype testing. The primary issues from the standpoint of anchor performance are ultimate capacity under monotonic loading and accumulation of permanent displacements under cyclic loading, which could potentially result in a loss of embedment. Since realistic loading conditions are critical to assessment of anchor performance, numerical simulations of wave and wind loading were conducted for a broad range of platform types and sizes, water depths, and environmental conditions. Anchor performance was verified through finite element (FE) and plastic limit analysis (PLA) numerical simulations in conjunction with parallel experimental studies with a geotechnical centrifuge. The centrifuge test program comprised four major components: monotonic loading in sand and clay and cyclic loading in sand and clay. Centrifuge testing of monotonic loading, Figure 1, investigated the influence of anchor embedment depth and load inclination angle on anchor load capacity. Application of omni-directional loading in the centrifuge tests involved developing the novel actuator assembly shown in Figure 2. This actuator system was used to apply the numerical predictions of mooring line load histories during a storm event (Figure 3) to the MRA. Figure 4 shows typical centrifuge test measurements of anchor displacement and trajectory due to applied loads. The cyclic centrifuge tests using line tensions from the environmental load numerical simulations largely show that the shared ring anchor can withstand expected loads while experiencing small displacements. The tests also reveal that shared anchors are likely to experience more deformations than single-line systems, due to changes in the load angle during different storm events. In addition to the technical accomplishments of this research related to evaluating the performance of the MRA under monotonic and cyclic loading in sands and clays, significant strides were made on advancing the transfer of this technology to industry. Major commercialization efforts of the MRA conducted during the duration of this project include participation in the NSF I-Corps program, medium scale basin tests conducted under the auspices of the NSF Partnership for Innovation Program, formation of a start-up company named Deep Anchor Solutions, further technical development of the MRA supported by a Small Business Innovation Research grant, and field testing at two National Geotechnical Engineering Sites: a clay site at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and a sand site at Texas A&M University.

abstractText:
Well-documented biases in hiring and admissions decisions often prevent qualified individuals from participating in the workforce and in education. Many current attempts to address this problem focus on reducing “implicit” or “unconscious” bias. At the same time, scientists are increasingly debating and critiquing implicit bias as a concept. While awareness of implicit biases has become commonplace, the associated science does not yet provide a solid foundation on which to build intervention efforts. The central goal of this project is to strengthen the scientific understanding of implicit bias by identifying differences in how people respond to groups and group labels, versus specific individuals and individual targets. It will reveal whether researchers and organizations wishing to address bias should be focusing on “unconscious” bias, or whether more effective interventions could be designed by focusing on bias toward groups versus individuals. The project will help address popular misconceptions of implicit bias from our theoretical understanding of how bias operates. In addition, it will generate valuable insights for addressing bias in real-world settings.

This project involves 12 experiments that will tackle a key confound that obstructs the ability to draw strong conclusions about the research on implicit bias: the confound between type of measure (i.e., explicit vs. implicit) and stimuli type (i.e., categories vs. exemplars). Traditionally, research examining explicit bias typically requires participants to respond to abstract social categories (e.g., the categories Black people and White people), whereas implicit measures typically involve specific exemplars of those categories (e.g., faces of Black and White individuals). The current project uses computer-based reaction time tasks and behavioral measures to probe core themes regarding implicit-explicit relations. For example, do low correlations between common implicit and explicit measures of bias reflect (a) differences in processing awareness or do those low correlations derive from (b) the differences in stimuli type? Moreover, do category-focused evaluations and exemplar-focused evaluations have distinct consequences? By identifying the distinction between explicit and implicit measures on the one hand, and the distinction between categories and exemplars on the other, we can gain new insights into the causes and consequences of bias, with important implications for both theory, practice, and discrimination intervention programs.

In total, this award supported 8 journal publications, plus a ninth currently under review. The central goal of this project was to strengthen the scientific understanding of asymmetrical responses to categories. Researchers have developed multiple ways to assess people’s responses to categories. For example, some measures capture fast, split-second reactions whereas others capture slower, more reflective reactions. Meanwhile, some measures capture people’s reactions to a general or abstract way of thinking about a category (e.g., a category label, like “chairs”), whereas other measures capture people’s reactions to specific examples of a category (e.g., a series of pictures of particular chairs).

In one paper, we examined two of the most common split-second measures of responses to categories that confound speed of measurement with type of stimulus. We found that this confound seemed potentially important for the most popular measure, whereas it seemed to play a relatively minor role for the other measure. These findings raise important questions about whether previously obtained dissociations between speeded and non-speeded measures of category responding are driven by the nature of the measurement instrument or by the particular stimuli scientists happened to use in these studies. 

In other papers, we examined measures that focus on people’s ideas about what they like or dislike as well as measures that capture their experiences of liking/disliking. For example, we found that people’s abstract ideas about what they like were only loosely connected to their concrete experiences of liking. Instead, their abstract ideas were influenced by subtle features of the situation. We also found that these two kinds of preferences guide different kinds of decisions. General ideas about liking helped predict choices made from a distance—such as deciding whether to join a website based only on its description. In contrast, concrete experiences of liking better predicted choices made after first-hand interaction—such as deciding whether to join a website after trying it out.

By carefully separating and examining these different factors, our project provides new insight into why asymmetric responses occur and what effects they have. These findings matter not only for improving scientific theories and measures, but also for how research using these kinds of measures is applied in real-world settings.
